title: The Western States 100-Mile Endurance Run: participation and performance trends
population: Starters and finishers of the Western States 100-Mile Endurance Run, 1974-2007
findings: Mean age of participants increased to around 45 years (P < 0.001), men being an average of 3 years older than women; the increase was accounted for by growth in participation among women aged 40+ and men 50+.
The average age of the top performers increased (P <= 0.002) since 1990 to the upper 30s for both sexes.
Fastest times among men were comparable across the 30-39 and 40-49 year age groups.
The authors conclude the fastest WSER runners are older than the ages at which the fastest marathons are run.
limitations: Race-level descriptive trends, finishers/participants only, no training or physiological data, 100-mile event in one mountainous course; no sample size in abstract.
implications: For 100-mile goals, men aged 40-49 ran comparably to those aged 30-39 at the front of this race, so no age-based target penalty before about 50 for ultra goals is a reasonable default (low confidence, cross-sectional).
Supports a later age-of-best-performance for 100-mile than marathon in this dataset; do not copy marathon age curves to 100-mile goals.
